transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Head of ML, NovaPayments), Marcus Chen (CTO), Liam O'Neill (SRE)

Summary: quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize focusing on batching and caching (prefix + KV), cost model examples for payment chat assistant, and next steps for pilot.

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick intro, i'm Sofia, AE on Redwood, with Ethan our SE.
[00:08] Priya: Hi, Priya here. We're excited, been reading the docs.
[00:12] Ethan: Awesome, we'll do a short demo, then dig into batching/k v cache tradeoffs and cost examples. Quick ask — what's your main goal for this pilot?
[00:22] Priya: Reduce per-conversation token costs while keeping 95th latency under 350ms for our realtime chat flow. We have a lot of repeated prefixes — e.g., account context — across sessions.
[00:34] Marcus: Also need SOC2 and KMS for keys, and regional data residency for EU traffic.
[00:40] Ethan: Totally, we support SAML SSO, KMS, and have private deploy options — we'll share the security pack. Back to batching: basic idea is we can batch tokens across concurrent requests to amortize kernel costs. In practice you get better throughput; latency impact depends on your batching window.
[01:05] Liam: Can you quantify that? We can't add more than ~40ms P95.
[01:09] Ethan: Sure — approximate numbers from similar customers: small adaptive batching (20-50ms collection window) adds ~5-30ms on average but improves throughput 2–4x depending on concurrency. If you need strict P95 we can do dynamic batching with latency caps and fall back to lower-latency nodes.
[01:30] Priya: And caching? We have repeated system prompts and user account metadata repeated across messages.
[01:36] Ethan: Two layers: prefix (session-level) cache and KV (key-value) cache for arbitrary subsequences. Prefix caching stores the initial token prefixes/KV cache saves and reuses KV cache states across sessions when keys match. Hit rates vary — for conversational payments flows we've seen prefix hit rates 40–70% if session structure is consistent. KV cache helps when you have reuse of large partial contexts — think invoice templates.
[02:05] Priya: What's difference in cost savings?
[02:07] Ethan: Rough model: each token emitted costs compute proportional to sequence length minus cache hits. With a 50% effective hit rate on a 200-token response, you effectively cut the generating-side tokens by ~50% — so large cost savings. We ran a simple exemplar: no cache cost = $0.020 per full session, with prefix cache 50% hit -> $0.011 per session. Numbers vary with model size and quantization.
[02:35] Marcus: Are there storage costs for KV cache or extra infra?
[02:39] Ethan: Minimal for managed; KV cache entries are stored in memory on serving nodes; for Dedicated we give options to persist to customer-managed Redis or our managed KV. Storage cost is typically small relative to GPU. For private deployments you can point to your Redis in VPC.
[02:56] Priya: How do you handle cold starts? If a user is new the cache misses a lot.
[03:01] Ethan: We handle cold-starts with prefix fallbacks and aggressive per-user warming where we can prefetch likely prefixes. Hit rates ramp up after a couple exchanges. During pilot we'll measure warm vs cold percentages and tune TTLs.
[03:18] [00:03:20] Sofia: Quick demo slide: here is the Optimize dashboard — we show token-level breakdown by route, cache hit rate, and a cost-savings simulator.
[03:30] [00:03:30] Ethan: Live example: sample conversation where prefix hits reduce KV size. Note: transcript text may have small transcription errors like 'k v cache' shown as 'K V cache'.
[03:46] Priya: On the cost model spreadsheet, can you walk through assumptions?
[03:50] Ethan: Sure — we assume model = 7B quantized, avg response 180 tokens, request-concat 30 tokens, concurrency 60 rps. Batching adds 15ms average; prefix hit rate 50% gives 48% token cost reduction. If we move to Dedicated with higher batching we get additional 1.6x throughput improvement.
[04:14] Marcus: What's the tradeoff of more aggressive batching?
[04:17] Ethan: Higher batching increases tail latency. For example, very aggressive batching to fill big batch sizes at low concurrency can add 100-200ms. That’s why we recommend dynamic policies: latency-first for payments route, cost-first for async jobs like reconciliation.
[04:35] Liam: How about functional correctness — do cached prefixes change output quality?
[04:39] Ethan: Good question. Prefix caching only caches KV state (keys/attn caches); it doesn't rewrite prompts. You may see slight variation if model internals rely on full historical context, but in practice we tune cache TTLs to maintain quality and run evals against prompt sets. We also provide regression alerts tied to eval sets.
[05:05] [00:05:05] Priya: For our compliance team, we need audit logs for every cache eviction and KMS usage.
[05:11] Sofia: We capture cache metrics and eviction events in the Console; audit trails for KMS operations are integrated when you use your customer-managed KMS. We'll include the SOC2 and audit doc.
[05:23] Marcus: If we go Dedicated, what's the onboarding time?
[05:26] Sofia: For Dedicated, 4–6 weeks typical including capacity sizing, private networking, and security review. Hosted pilot can start in 1–2 weeks.
[05:34] Priya: We want to try hosted pilot first to validate hit rates and unit economics.
[05:38] Ethan: Makes sense. Pilot plan we discussed: 2-week pilot with traffic replay, measurement of hit rates, P95 latency, and cost per session. We'll run the benchmark script and a real traffic replay.
[05:52] [00:05:52] Transcript oddity: overlapping talk, Liam briefly cuts in: 'what about eviction policy'
[06:00] Ethan: eviction policy — LRU by default, TTLs configurable per-customer route, and you can pin keys for sticky contexts.
[06:10] Priya: Do you support per-route policies? We want low-latency routing for login flows, cost-optimized for receipts generation.
[06:16] Ethan: Yes per-route policies in Console. You can set batching window, cache TTL, and preferred model variants per route.
[06:24] Marcus: Can you show a simple cost calc: 1M sessions per month, avg 1.2 requests per session, avg 200 resp tokens?
[06:31] Ethan: Quick back-of-envelope: without caching, token compute = 1M * 1.2 * 200 = 240M tokens. If price/kg = $0.000085 per token compute (placeholder), cost = ~$20.4k. With 50% effective cache -> 120M tokens -> ~$10.2k. Add infra and storage ~1-2k. We'll send a detailed spreadsheet.
[06:55] Priya: Those numbers look promising. For QA, can we run the bench with our anonymized traffic?
[06:59] Ethan: Absolutely, we'll provide the benchmark script and instructions to sanitize traces.
[07:04] Sofia: Next steps recap — we'll send pilot SOW and pricing, security pack, and the benchmark script. Can we set target date for kickoff?
[07:11] Priya: Prefer Monday Dec 14, but we'll try earlier; we'll share run windows.
[07:15] Marcus: Also want to include SRE on the kickoff.
[07:18] Liam: I'll be on it.
[07:20] [00:07:20] Sofia: Great, action items — Ethan shares scripts, Sofia sends SOW/pricing, Redwood security sends SOC2/KMS notes.
[07:30] Priya: couple final quick Qs — do you support model pinning during rollouts?
[07:33] Ethan: Yes, rollouts with canary and automatic fallback to older model variants if quality regressions detected.
[07:40] Priya: ok great, that's it from me.
[07:42] Sofia: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials and calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
